Integrated Circuit Design & Computing Architectures

Timing-Driven Datapath Optimization of a Vector Shifter Unit

▸

Restructured the leading-sign-bit counting logic and the barrel shifter inside a vector shifter module of an AI accelerator to meet timing. Verified the unit using a Cocotb block-level testbench, which was also used to debug the design while restructuring it. Synthesized and optimized using Synopsys Fusion Compiler.

Key Improvements
  • Dedicated datapaths: The earlier design used one shared datapath for different instruction types, which created a long critical path through all the logic in the shared datapath, even though no single instruction type functionally uses all of that logic. Each instruction type now has its own dedicated datapath, removing the logic that is not needed for that specific instruction type.
  • Barrel shifter refactoring: Restructured the shifter so each stage works on narrower data where possible, with an enable/disable mechanism that turns off idle logic. Also reworked the critical path for the wider data format: since the unit supports floating-point precision only for a narrower format, shift propagation for the wider format is defined separately and broken into shorter segments.
Results
Leading-sign logic (normal)0.30 ns to 0.15 ns (50% improvement)
Leading-sign logic (floating point)0.30 ns to 0.21 ns (30% improvement)
Barrel shifter (worst path)0.36 ns to 0.30 ns (16.7% improvement)
Area utilization+2 to 3% over original

RTL Analysis, Verification & Genus Synthesis of UETRV-Pcore (RV32IMA) Across Multi-PVT Corners (FYDP)

▸
Overview

Did the design documentation of the UETRV-Pcore (documentation link). Did RTL block-level verification of the core memory modules (icache, dcache and MMU) using two methods. Also ran synthesis of the core using Cadence Genus.

Verification methods
  • SystemVerilog testbenches: Target the verification of basic functionality of the RTL blocks.
  • Python Cocotb framework: Randomized data is given to the blocks to test them in bulk.
Findings

Found an anomaly with the replacement policy of the icache: the replacement pointer increments by 1 on every memory acknowledgement signal, regardless of whether the address belongs to the same cache line.

Power and Timing Tradeoffs
  • Power scales almost linearly with frequency (about 1.1 W at 100 MHz to 3.6 W at 300 MHz in ss) and rises with supply voltage, from 1.12 W at ss to 1.90 W at ff for 100 MHz.
  • Timing is limited by the slowest corner: ss meets timing only at 100 MHz, tt at up to 200 MHz, and ff at all three frequencies (up to 300 MHz).
  • Pushing frequency past what a corner can sustain only adds power without closing timing, so ss sets the achievable frequency while ff sets the power budget.

Local-to-Shared Register File Coherency Verification and Debug in an AI Accelerator

▸
Overview

In the accelerator's compute architecture, each processing element has a small local register file to reduce memory latency, backed by a larger shared vector register file. A coherence mechanism keeps the two consistent. I verified that this mechanism worked correctly, debugged the existing implementation, and extended it to cover missing cases.

Data representation handling

Added missing cases in the checking logic so that data is always held in the correct format inside the local register file.

Hazard handling

Implemented a fix for a read-after-write (RAW) hazard between consecutive dependent instructions.

Data transfer between register files

Added missing cases that trigger transfers between the local and shared register files at the correct time, keeping data consistent.

Register renaming

Extended the renaming policy to cover missing corner cases involving register conflicts.

RISC-V Microbenchmarking on UETRV-Pcore for IPC (Instructions Per Cycle)-Level Performance Evaluation

▸
Overview

Evaluated the performance of the UETRV-Pcore, a five-stage RV32IMAZicsr core without a branch predictor, using microbenchmarks from the riscv-validation repository. The benchmarks cover control flow, dependency chains, memory load/store operations and integer arithmetic. Measured IPC with and without compiler optimization to identify microarchitectural bottlenecks.

Methodology
  • Compilation: Benchmarks were compiled with the riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc toolchain at -O0 and -O1. The -O1, -O2 and -O3 levels gave very similar IPC, so only -O0 and -O1 are reported.
  • Simulation: The RTL was simulated cycle-accurately with Verilator. Binaries were converted to .hex with a Python script.
  • Measurement: The source was instrumented to read the mcycle and minstret CSRs before and after each benchmark, and the counts were sent out over UART for IPC calculation.
Results

Findings
  • No branch predictor: Branch outcomes are resolved in the execute stage, so taken branches flush the fetch and decode stages and waste cycles. This keeps IPC low for control-heavy code.
  • Load-use RAW hazard: An instruction that depends on a preceding load stalls for one cycle, because the load result is not available when it reaches execute. This makes dependent loads the worst memory case.
  • Compiler optimization: Instruction scheduling and loop transformations lift dependency and arithmetic code to nearly 0.94 IPC. Memory-bound code stays limited by memory latency, which the compiler cannot remove.
  • Improvement direction: Adding a dynamic branch predictor would reduce pipeline flushes in control-intensive workloads.

End-to-End Linux Boot on UETRV-Pcore FPGA via OpenSBI and UART Image Transfer

▸
Overview

Booted Linux on the UETRV-Pcore with an FPGA as the target platform, using a carefully configured boot process.

Software Stack
  • Bootloader: OpenSBI 0.9 serves as the first-stage bootloader and provides the interface between the RISC-V hardware and the Linux kernel.
  • Root filesystem: Built with Buildroot 2021.05 using an initramfs-based configuration and BusyBox 1.33, which provides a lightweight set of essential Unix utilities for an efficient runtime environment.
  • Toolchain and kernel: Compiled with the GNU RISC-V toolchain (riscv32-unknown-linux-gnu). The Linux 6.1 kernel is integrated directly into OpenSBI as a payload, so OpenSBI loads it and transfers control during boot.
Image Transfer

The OS image, such as the Linux kernel binary, is sent from the host computer to the FPGA over a UART serial connection. The zero-stage bootloader on the target, stored in the boot memory (bmem) of the UETRV-Pcore, receives the image and writes it to the designated memory region. Once the transfer is complete, it starts executing the loaded image, completing the Linux bootstrapping process.

Host Communication

The FPGA board's USB interface is connected to the host and provides access to the UART serial interface. On the host, GTKTerm is used as the serial terminal to monitor the UART output of the UETRV-Pcore, so boot messages and Linux console output from the SiFive-compatible UART can be observed during boot.

Boot Flow

The FPGA runs the UETRV-Pcore hardware, the processor executes OpenSBI, OpenSBI transfers control to the Linux 6.1 kernel, and the kernel uses the configured SiFive UART to provide console output to the host PC, where it is monitored through GTKTerm.

Resources

The configuration files for Buildroot, BusyBox, Linux, and OpenSBI are provided in this Google Drive folder, along with guidelines for the overall flow.

Timing Closure at Place-and-Route (PnR) Stage for 12LPP AI Accelerator Using Synopsys Fusion Compiler

▸
Overview

Ran static timing analysis on the different design blocks of an AI accelerator and its CPU, analyzing the critical paths of each block against a threshold of 45 logic levels, and worked on the paths that exceeded it.

Techniques

Resolved the critical paths using retiming, mux segmentation, and restructuring. Retiming was the primary solution, applying cutset retiming, the node transfer theorem, and the delay transfer theorem. Mux segmentation addressed high fan-out issues, for example in the Vector Permutation Unit, where a single 2048-bit mux was broken down into 128-bit muxes using hierarchical tree decomposition.

Workflow

Analyzed the timing reports, then examined the timing path before the launch flip-flop and the timing path of the capture flip-flop on each critical path to identify where retiming could apply. After retiming or another fix, reran physical synthesis and re-checked timing using Fusion Compiler.

Design optimization

In some cases the fix went beyond retiming. In the scalar unit, a divide operator left slack between -50 ps and -90 ps across the different start and end points passing through that operator, with 55+ logic levels; replacing it with a shift operation brought slack into the -15 ps to -10 ps range with logic levels under 45.

Results
Vector Floating Point Unit slack closed to~ -1 ps
Vector Permutation Unit slack closed to~ 0 ps
Scalar Unit slack closed to-15 to -10 ps
Logic levels, all blocksWithin 45

Clock and Reset Domain Crossing (CDC/RDC) Verification Using Synopsys SpyGlass

▸
Overview

Performed rigorous Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) and Reset Domain Crossing (RDC) verification on a complex SoC subsystem to ensure robust multi-clock reliability and asynchronous safety. Using SpyGlass, the verification process systematically identified structural flaws, missing constraints, and synchronization gaps across deeply nested hardware hierarchies, followed by targeted fixes, architectural waivers, and constraint updates.

Issues and resolutions
  • Clock constraints and definitions: The tool flagged unconstrained root and gated clocks operating within internal modules. Added explicit clock definitions and period constraints to the system's Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) files to establish clear timing baselines.
  • Reset polarity and declaration management: Resets were either undeclared, improperly bounded, or triggered mismatch errors due to inverted active-high versus active-low logic expectations. Corrected reset assertions, explicitly mapped control polarities, and properly declared asynchronous resets within the reset constraint configurations.
  • Asynchronous data and control paths: These paths triggered warnings because the automated checkers could not fully verify complex handshaking or custom synchronization structures out of the box. Evaluated the flagged paths and classified them as false positives, confirming that they safely adhered to Control-Synchronizer-with-Data-Hold behavior.
  • Reset Domain Crossing (RDC) and soft resets: Cascaded pipeline stages were used as reset synchronizers, so their outputs were treated as soft resets by the tool. Defined custom soft-reset handling rules to resolve this issue.
Synopsys SpyGlass

Physical Design Constraint Verification for Physical Synthesis Flow Using Synopsys TCM

▸
Overview

Verified the constraints used in the physical synthesis (PnR) of the core, using Synopsys Fishtail for timing constraint management, and resolved the large majority of the flagged issues directly.

Issue categories analyzed

Covered setup issues (RTL, SDC, and IO issues), clock generation verification issues, clock distribution and propagation issues, multicycle path issues, and false path issues.

Resolutions

Some of the issues that I resolved are:

  • Waived issues originating from Synopsys IPs.
  • Clock input transition / driving cell issue: no input transition or driving cell was defined for clocks, so defined the driving cell and clock transition for them.
  • Missing IO delays: several ports had no input/output delays defined, so defined them.
  • Multi-clock IO delay issue: with more than one clock in the design, IO delays needed to be defined relative to each clock using the -add option, which was missing, so added it.
  • Static signal issue: static input/output signals that were not relative to the clock still had input/output delays defined, so implemented a false path on the static input signals and applied set_case_analysis on the static output signals after removing their output delays.
  • Cross-checked every error and its resolution against Synopsys's official documentation.
Results
  • Achieved 100% constraint mapping across all 13 RTL blocks in the design.
  • Observed a tool bug related to an SDC issue and filed a SolvNet case with Synopsys, providing sample code to help reproduce it. Synopsys was able to reproduce the error on their side using the sample code and filed a JIRA for it.

Testing & Hardware Verification

Sv32 Virtual Memory Verification via RISCOF-Based Exception and PTE Bit Test Development

▸
Overview

Checked how faithfully the Sv32 virtual memory subsystem follows the RISC-V specification, in particular how it handles the permission bits in page table entries (PTEs).

Test Development
  • Directed assembly tests: Wrote custom RISC-V assembly tests that systematically change the permission bits in the PTEs and then access memory under different privilege modes.
  • Page table setup: Used a two-level page table, where the first level is called level 1 and the second level is called level 0.
  • Build: Compiled the tests with the GNU toolchain.
Cross-Simulator Comparison

Used the Sail RISC-V model as the golden reference model. Ran the tests on both the Spike and Sail simulators through the RISCOF framework and compared the log files from the two. Any mismatch in memory access behavior points to an inconsistency that needs investigation.

Reporting

Collected the results in an HTML report that shows how each permission bit affects virtual memory behavior across privilege modes. The study gives more confidence in how virtual memory behavior is modeled and simulated for RISC-V.

Clock Gating Activity Verification Using Firmware-Driven Core Execution and External Signal Monitoring

▸
Overview

Analyzed all the clock gates in the vector compute units and verified that each block's clock is enabled only while it is needed.

Test Design
  • Assembly test: Wrote an assembly test containing all the vector instructions associated with each specific block. Instructions of different blocks that do not depend on each other are issued in parallel, so to test each block's clock gating inside a single test, 20 scalar instructions are inserted after every block's instruction before the next vector instruction of a different block. This prevents the next vector instruction from being issued in parallel with the previous block's instruction.
  • Reference cycle counts: Used the mcycle CSR inside the assembly test to count the reference number of cycles for each vector instruction.
  • External driver: Wrote an external driver to analyze DUT signals and verify the activity of the clock gates.
Checks
  • Clock enable timing: Validated, using SystemVerilog Assertions, that the clock gate of the associated RTL block turns on exactly one cycle after the instruction is issued.
  • Other blocks gated: Validated that while an instruction of a specific block executes, the clocks of the other blocks stay gated.
  • Clock-on duration: Compared the number of gated-clock cycles of each block with the reference cycle count, to confirm the clock is enabled for exactly the required time span and not longer.
Findings

In the parallel processing compute units, the clocks are also enabled for the instructions of other vector blocks, so there is no granularity in enabling the clocks for them.

Publications

2026
RTL Analysis and Genus Synthesis of UETRV-Pcore
Zia, Murad, Nadeem, Ijaz, in Elektron Magazine, Vol. 9, Issue 3

This project presents RTL analysis and Cadence Genus synthesis of the Pcore, a RISC-V-based processor core. The work involved detailed documentation of internal modules, focusing on pinouts, interconnections, and logic flow. Memory modules were verified using SystemVerilog testbenches in QuestaSim and randomized bulk testing via the Cocotb Python framework. Synthesis was performed under three PVT corners (ss, tt, ff) and multiple frequencies (100 to 300 MHz) to evaluate timing, area, and power trade-offs. The ss corner ensured timing reliability, ff enabled power profiling, and tt provided balanced performance metrics. The complete workflow reflects practical RTL-to-synthesis design using industry-standard tools.

2026
Performance Evaluation of the UETRV-Pcore using RISC-V Microbenchmarks
Zia, in IJEAST, Vol. 10, Issue 10, p1–6

Evaluates the UETRV-Pcore, a five-stage RV32IMAZicsr RISC-V core with Sv32 virtual memory and FPGA deployment support, using standardized microbenchmarks covering control flow, dependency chains, memory operations, and arithmetic workloads. Measures Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) across compiler optimization levels to expose microarchitectural bottlenecks: unoptimized code averages around 0.5 IPC, while compiler-driven scheduling and loop transformations lift execution-heavy benchmarks to roughly 0.94 IPC. Memory-bound benchmarks remain constrained by read-after-write hazards and the absence of dynamic branch prediction, pointing to a hardware branch predictor as the clearest next improvement.

2023
Virtual Memory Verification Sv32
Ali, Zia, Kamal, Azhar, in Elektron Magazine, Vol. 6, Issue 3, p12–14

Virtual memory compliance refers to the extent to which the behaviour of the virtual memory subsystem adheres to the specifications outlined in the RISC-V architecture. It ensures that the behavior of virtual memory operations, particularly the manipulation of permission bits within page table entries, aligns accurately with the documented expectations and standards of the RISC-V architecture. We developed customized RISC-V assembly tests that systematically modify permission bits within page table entries. These tests are compiled using GNU toolchain and executed using the RISC-V assembly code on both the Spike and Sail simulators through the RISCOF framework, facilitating cross-platform analysis. By comparing the resulting log files from the two simulators, we discern any inconsistencies or variations in memory access behaviors. The findings of this investigation provide insights into the fidelity of RISC-V architecture specifications with respect to virtual memory operations. We generally worked with two level page table in which first level is named as level 1 and second level is named as level 0. These outcomes are synthesized into a comprehensive HTML report, offering an in-depth exploration of permission bit effects on virtual memory within varying privilege modes. This research enhances comprehension of virtual memory functionality in the RISC-V architecture. This study contributes to a more robust understanding of virtual memory behavior and engenders confidence in the modeling and simulation of such systems.
